mainTopic: What lets a debt be collected from sold property (fixed amount, writing, or timing), and the oath of one who finds a lost object.
overview: The גמרא asks what an obligation needs in order to be collected from property already sold to a buyer (נכסים משועבדים): must it be both fixed in amount and written down, or is a fixed amount enough? It first tries to prove this from a daughter's dowry (פרנסה), which is fixed but unwritten. The proof is rejected, because a dowry is public knowledge and so counts as written. רב הונא בר מנוח then brings a משנה in which a stepdaughter collects food support even from buyers. The גמרא explains that a קנין was made for her, and after several attempts settles on why the man's own daughter does not collect this way: her father may already have given her money. Next a teaching of רבי נתן suggests that collecting from buyers depends only on timing. The גמרא answers that תנאים disagree, some saying the reason is that these debts are unwritten and רבי יוסי saying it is that they are unfixed. Finally, the גמרא turns to the משנה's rule that a finder of a lost object does not swear. It brings רבי יצחק's cases of tied pouches and tied oxen, then challenges how he can require an oath at all.

steps.title: The second side of the question: is a fixed amount enough?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its question by giving the other option: maybe a fixed amount is enough to collect from sold property, even without a written document.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps it is enough that the amount is fixed, even if it is not written down?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question it started just before this. It gives the second option: maybe an obligation only needs a set amount, and does not need to be written, to be collected from property that was sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, the גמרא asked whether an obligation must be both קצובין (a set amount) and כתובין (written down) to be collected from משועבדים. Now it offers the second side: maybe קצובין alone is enough. The rest of this section tries to settle which side is correct.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps (introduces the second side of a question)
Fixed, set in amount
Written down in a document
Property that was sold but still carries a lien, so a creditor can take it from the buyer

phrases.english: Or perhaps it is enough that they are fixed,
even though they are not written?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided question that began before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether being fixed in amount is enough to collect from sold property, or whether the obligation must also be written.

steps.title: Bringing a case: two daughters, a son, and the dowry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a case to help answer the question. A man left two daughters and a son. The first daughter took her tenth as a dowry, and then the son died before the second daughter took hers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear what was taught: A man died and left two daughters and a son. The first daughter went ahead and took a tenth of the property. The second daughter did not manage to collect hers before the son died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof by describing a case. The ruling on this case comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A daughter is owed a dowry of a tenth of her father's estate, collected from the son who inherits. Here the son died, so the whole estate now passes to the two daughters. The open question is whether the second daughter still gets her tenth first, before the rest is split equally.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source that may answer the question)
It was stated (a teaching of the אמוראים)
A tenth of the estate, the standard dowry for an orphaned daughter
To collect

phrases.english: Come and hear, for it was stated:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁמֵּת וְהִנִּיחַ שְׁתֵּי בָּנוֹת וּבֵן,
phrases.english: One who died and left two daughters and a son,
and the first daughter went ahead and took a tenth of the property,
phrases.notes: This tenth is her dowry, taken from the estate that the son inherited.

phrases.english: and the second daughter did not manage to collect
before the son died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a case that may answer the question from step 1.
steps.raayaObject: The question of whether a fixed but unwritten obligation can be collected from sold property.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case of the two daughters and the son, discussed by רבי יוחנן and רבי חנינא.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the second daughter gave up her share
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that the second daughter lost her right to first take a tenth as a dowry.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: The second daughter gave up her share.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives his ruling: since the second daughter did not collect her tenth before the son died, she no longer gets it separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In his view, she now simply splits the estate equally with her sister. She does not get an extra tenth first. Her dowry right is not treated as something already attached to the property.

keyTerms.meaning: She gave up, forfeited

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
The second one gave up her share.
phrases.notes: He means she loses the extra tenth, and the two sisters just split the estate equally.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives one אמורא's ruling on the case from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second daughter has given up her separate tenth.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: a dowry can even be taken from buyers
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא challenges רבי יוחנן. A dowry is so strong that it can be taken back even from people who bought the father's property, while food support cannot. So how can the second daughter lose it?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said to him: They said even more than this. We take property away from buyers for a daughter's dowry, though not for her food. And you say the second daughter gave up her share?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא attacks רבי יוחנן's ruling. He points to a known rule showing that a daughter's dowry right is very strong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the son sold the father's property, the daughter can take it from the buyer to pay her dowry. So the dowry is like a lien on the property. If it can be taken even from an outsider, it should surely be taken from the estate before the sisters divide it.

keyTerms.meaning: Even more than this (a stronger case)
We take away from buyers
A daughter's dowry
Food support

steps.confusionAlert: Here פַּרְנָסָה means the daughter's dowry, not 'making a living.' And מְזוֹנוֹת means her food support. The two have different rules.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chanina said to him,
They said something even greater than this:
We take away property from buyers for a dowry,
but we do not take it away for food support;
and you say the second one gave up her share?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי חֲנִינָא, גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ אָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's ruling in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the second daughter gave up her tenth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dowry can be taken even from outside buyers. It should certainly be taken from the estate before the heirs divide it.

steps.title: The proof: a dowry is fixed but not written, and still collected
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws its point. A dowry is a fixed amount but is not written in any document, and רבי חנינא says it can still be taken from buyers. So a fixed amount seems to be enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a dowry is fixed, yet it is not written, and still she takes it from buyers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to its question from step 1. It uses רבי חנינא's rule as evidence that a fixed amount is enough, even without writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A dowry is always a set amount, one tenth, but no document records it. Since רבי חנינא says it can be taken from sold property, writing does not seem to be required. This supports the second side of the question.

keyTerms.meaning: It is indeed fixed
It is not written

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי חנינא, a dowry is fixed (a tenth) and unwritten, yet it can be taken from buyers. This seems to show that being fixed is enough, but the next step rejects this proof.

phrases.english: But look at a dowry:
it is indeed fixed,
but it is not written;
and yet she takes it away from buyers!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes רבי חנינא's statement from step 4 and applies it to the question in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: The view that a fixed but unwritten obligation can be collected from sold property.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חנינא's rule that a dowry, which is fixed but unwritten, can be taken from buyers.

steps.title: A dowry is different because everyone knows about it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 5. A dowry is public knowledge, so it is treated as if it were written. This means the dowry case does not prove that a fixed amount alone is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: A dowry is different. Since it has publicity, it is treated like something written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof it just made. It says the dowry case is special, so we cannot learn from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 argued that a dowry is fixed but unwritten, yet it can be collected from buyers. Now the גמרא says the dowry really does have something like writing: everyone knows a man's daughters get a dowry from his estate. So buyers were on notice, and the case may still need both a fixed amount and writing (or its equal).

keyTerms.meaning: It is different
Here: a daughter's dowry (the tenth of the estate)
Publicity; something people know about
It is treated as if it were written

steps.confusionAlert: In this סוגיא פַּרְנָסָה does not mean 'livelihood.' It means the dowry a daughter takes from her father's estate. Food support is called מְזוֹנוֹת.

phrases.english: A dowry is different,
since it has publicity,
phrases.notes: People know a man's daughters will take a dowry from his property, so a buyer can't say he was surprised.

phrases.english: it is like something written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 5 by showing the dowry has a special feature.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the dowry. It does not decide the original question.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dowry is not truly 'unwritten,' because its publicity works like writing. So it cannot prove that a fixed amount alone is enough.

steps.title: A stepdaughter's food support is collected even from sold property
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח brings a משנה. A stepdaughter whose stepfathers promised to feed her can collect even from sold property, because she is like a creditor. Her support is neither fixed nor written, so this seems to contradict the idea that collecting needs a fixed amount or writing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר מנוח objected: If the husbands died, their own daughters are fed only from unsold property. But she (the stepdaughter) is fed even from sold property, because she is like a creditor!
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בר מנוח challenges the whole discussion with a משנה. In it, a stepdaughter collects food support even from property that was sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husbands' own daughters get food support only from unsold property, which fits the usual rule. But the stepdaughter was promised food by agreement, so she counts as a creditor and can collect even from buyers. Her food support has no fixed amount and was not written, so this seems to clash with both sides of the question.

keyTerms.meaning: He raises an objection (usually from a משנה or ברייתא)
Are fed; receive food support
Free property; property not sold
Liened property that has been sold to others
A creditor (female)

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Manoach raised an objection:
If they died, their daughters are fed
phrases.notes: 'They' are two husbands who each promised to feed the woman's daughter from an earlier marriage (כתובות 101b).

phrases.english: from unsold property,
but she is fed even from sold property,
phrases.notes: 'She' is the stepdaughter, the one the husbands promised to feed.

phrases.english: because she is like a creditor!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the dowry proof was set aside, a new source is brought that seems to cut against the required conditions.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that collecting from sold property needs a fixed amount and/or a written document.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The stepdaughter's food support is neither a fixed amount nor written, yet the משנה lets her collect it from buyers.

steps.title: The case is where a formal קנין was made
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה speaks of a case where a קנין was done to confirm the promise. That makes it strong like a written debt, so it can be collected from buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where they made a קנין from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב הונא בר מנוח's challenge by narrowing the case in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stepdaughter collects from sold property only because the promise was sealed with a formal act of acquisition (קנין). A קנין makes the debt as strong and known as a written one. So the משנה does not prove that an unfixed, unwritten debt can be collected from buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
They made a קנין from him; a formal act that seals a commitment

steps.whatToRemember: A dowry counts as 'written' because it is public. A stepdaughter's support can be collected from buyers only when a קנין sealed the promise. So both sources may still require writing or something just as strong.

phrases.english: Here, what case are we dealing with?
Where they made a kinyan from him.
phrases.notes: A formal act was done to lock in the husband's promise to feed the girl, so it is as strong as a written debt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by limiting the משנה to a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stepdaughter collects from buyers even though her support is unfixed and unwritten.
steps.terutzMaskana: She collects from buyers only because a קנין sealed the promise, which works like writing.

steps.title: Then the man's own daughters should collect too
steps.stepSummary: If a קנין makes support strong enough to collect from buyers, the man's own daughters (בנות) should also be able to collect their support from sold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the daughters too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 8. If a קנין is what lets the stepdaughter collect from buyers, then the man's own daughters should be able to do the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 explained that the stepdaughter collects from sold property because a קנין made her support strong. But the rule is that a man's own daughters (בנות) do not collect their support from sold property. If a קנין was made, why shouldn't it help them too?

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if what you just said is true
Daughters, here meaning the man's own daughters
Also, too

phrases.english: If so, the daughters too!
phrases.notes: He means the man's own daughters should also collect their support from sold property, just like the stepdaughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer from step 8 (that a קנין was done)
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a קנין makes the stepdaughter's support collectible from buyers
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a קנין makes support strong, the man's own daughters should benefit from it too. Yet they do not collect from sold property.

steps.title: The קנין was made only for the stepdaughter
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where a קנין was done for the stepdaughter, but not for the daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where they made a קנין for this one, and did not make a קנין for that one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that in this case the קנין was made only for the stepdaughter. No קנין was made for the man's own daughters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference has nothing to do with who the girls are. It is simply a fact about this case: only one girl received a קנין. So only her support can be collected from buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: They made a קנין (a formal act that makes a promise binding)
For this one

phrases.english: Where they made a קנין for this one,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the stepdaughter.

phrases.english: and did not make a קנין for that one.
phrases.notes: "That one" is the man's own daughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the קנין was made only for the stepdaughter
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A קנין was made for everyone, so the daughters should also collect from buyers
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the stepdaughter received a קנין, so only she collects from buyers

steps.title: Why set up the case this way?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the תנא would describe a case where a קנין was made for one girl and not for the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason for this fixed distinction?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the case would always split this way, with a קנין for the stepdaughter but not for the daughter. This question sets up the next step, which gives an explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10's answer sounds random, as if it just happened that one girl got a קנין. The גמרא wants a real reason why the stepdaughter would have a קנין and the daughter would not.

keyTerms.meaning: What makes this a fixed rule? Why is the case set up this way?

phrases.english: What is the fixed reason?
phrases.notes: Literally "what is decided?" He is asking why the case always comes out with a קנין for one girl and not the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reason behind the answer of step 10
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why would the קנין have been made for the stepdaughter and not for the man's own daughter?

steps.title: Only the stepdaughter was alive when the קנין was made
steps.stepSummary: The stepdaughter was already alive when the קנין was made, so it works for her. The man's own daughter was not yet born, so it does not work for her.
steps.simpleTranslation: His wife's daughter, who was alive at the time of the קנין, benefits from the קנין. His own daughter, who was not alive at the time of the קנין, does not benefit from the קנין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the difference is about timing. The stepdaughter already existed when the קנין was made, but the man's own daughter was born later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קנין can only work for someone who exists when it is made. The stepdaughter (בת אשתו) was born before this marriage, so she was there for the קנין. His own daughter (בתו) was born from this marriage, after the קנין was made.

keyTerms.meaning: His wife's daughter (from an earlier marriage), the stepdaughter
His own daughter
At the time the קנין was made
Works, takes effect

phrases.english: His wife's daughter, who was there at the time of the קנין:
the קנין works for her.
His own daughter, who was not there at the time of the קנין:
the קנין does not work for her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference is timing: the stepdaughter existed when the קנין was made, and the daughter did not yet exist.

steps.title: What if both girls were alive at the קנין?
steps.stepSummary: Sometimes both girls were alive when a קנין was made, for example if he divorced the mother and later remarried her. The timing answer cannot explain that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are we not also dealing with a case where both were there at the time of the קנין? How could that happen? Where he divorced her and took her back!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the timing answer from step 12. It points to a case where both girls were already alive when the קנין was made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose a man married the mother, had a daughter with her, divorced her, and then remarried her with a new קנין. Now both his daughter and the stepdaughter were alive at the new קנין. Since the rule that only the stepdaughter collects from buyers still applies, timing cannot be the real reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Are we not also dealing with...? (introduces a case the answer fails to cover)
Both of them
What is the case? How could it happen?
He divorced her and took her back

phrases.english: Are we not dealing
with a case where both of them were there at the time of the קנין?
And how could that be? Where he divorced her and took her back!
phrases.notes: When he remarried her, a new קנין was made, and by then his own daughter had already been born.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי לָא עָסְקִינַן דַּהֲווֹ תַּרְוַיְיהוּ בִּשְׁעַת קִנְיָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the timing answer of step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that only the stepdaughter was alive at the time of the קנין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In a divorce-and-remarriage case, both girls were alive at the new קנין. Timing therefore cannot explain why only the stepdaughter collects from buyers.

steps.title: The two girls get support for different reasons
steps.stepSummary: His own daughter gets support through a תנאי בית דין, so a קנין does not change her rights. The stepdaughter gets support only through a private promise, so the קנין strengthens it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: his own daughter, who eats (is supported) through a תנאי בית דין, does not benefit from the קנין. His wife's daughter, who does not eat through a תנאי בית דין, does benefit from the קנין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the timing answer and gives a new one. The difference is the source of each girl's right to support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A man's own daughter is supported because of a תנאי בית דין, a condition the court built into every marriage. Her support follows that rule's limits, and a קנין cannot change it. The stepdaughter has no such rule in her favor. Her support comes only from the husband's private promise, so a קנין on that promise makes it as strong as a debt, collectible even from buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the earlier answer and gives a new one)
A condition the court built into every marriage, even if it was never said
She eats, meaning she is supported

steps.whatToRemember: This answer says the difference is the source of each girl's right: a תנאי בית דין for the daughter, a private promise for the stepdaughter. The next step knocks it down, and step 16 gives the גמרא's final reason.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not the גמרא's final answer. Step 15 argues that this reasoning makes the daughter weaker than the stepdaughter, and step 16 replaces it.

phrases.english: Rather, his own daughter:
since she eats through a court condition,
phrases.notes: Her support was never really part of the husband's promise. The court's built-in rule gives it to her.

phrases.english: the קנין does not work for her;
his wife's daughter:
since she does not eat through a court condition,
the קנין works for her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בִּתּוֹ דְּבִתְנַאי בֵּית דִּין קָאָכְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Drops the timing answer rejected in step 13 and gives a new reason
steps.terutzResolutionType: New distinction based on where each girl's right to support comes from
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference depends on who was alive when the קנין was made
steps.terutzMaskana: The daughter's support comes from a תנאי בית דין, which a קנין cannot change. The stepdaughter's support comes from a private promise, which a קנין strengthens.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: This is not the final answer. Step 15 rejects it, and step 16 explains the difference instead with the worry that the father may already have given his daughter money (צררי אתפסה).

steps.title: Can an extra source of rights make her weaker?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks Step 14: the daughter has both a תנאי בית דין and a קנין, so she should not be worse off than the stepdaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: But does having an extra source of rights make her lose out?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 14. It asks how the daughter could be weaker when she has the תנאי בית דין and a קנין too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 said the קנין does nothing extra for the daughter because she already has a תנאי בית דין. The גמרא pushes back: at worst the קנין adds nothing, so it should still work for her at least as well as it works for the stepdaughter. Having two sources of rights cannot make her worse off than having one.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it really so? (opens a sharp question)
Does she lose out? Is she made weaker?
A formal act that makes an obligation binding

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the daughter has no rights. It is asking why her rights would be weaker than the stepdaughter's when she has even more backing.

phrases.english: But is she then made weaker?!
phrases.notes: He means: can the extra backing of the court's rule make the daughter worse off than the stepdaughter?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly attacks the answer given in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 14 that the קנין does not help the daughter because she already has a תנאי בית דין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two sources of rights cannot be weaker than one. The קנין should at least help her as much as it helps the stepdaughter.

steps.title: Maybe he already gave his daughter money
steps.stepSummary: The difference is a doubt: since the daughter gets support by the court's rule, maybe her father already gave her money during his life.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, with his daughter: since she eats based on a תנאי בית דין, we can say he may have already handed her bundles of money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. The problem with the daughter is not weaker rights, but a doubt that she may already have been paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A father supports his daughter under the תנאי בית דין, so it is normal that he might have given her money in advance for her needs. Because of this doubt, she cannot take land from buyers. With the stepdaughter there is no such worry, so with a קנין she can collect even from sold property.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the old answer and brings a new one)
She eats (she receives her support)
Say / we can suppose
Bundles of money
He handed over to her

steps.whatToRemember: The daughter cannot collect from sold property because we suspect her father already gave her money, not because her rights are weaker.

phrases.english: Rather, his daughter –
since she eats based on a stipulation of the court,
say he handed her bundles of money.
phrases.notes: He means the father may have already paid for her support while he was alive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer of Step 14 after Step 15 knocked it down.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reason for the difference between the two girls
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The daughter's rights are weaker because they come from a תנאי בית דין.
steps.terutzMaskana: The daughter's rights are not weaker; there is just a doubt that she was already paid, so buyers cannot be made to pay.

steps.title: רבי נתן: it depends on which came first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי נתן, who says a buyer can collect his improvements from sold property if the improvements came before the sale. This suggests the rule is only about timing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי נתן said: When is this so? When the second buyer's purchase came before the first buyer's improvements. But if the first buyer's improvements came before the second buyer's purchase, he collects from sold property. So it seems the reason is only that his claim did not come first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to challenge the reason for the rule about sold property. רבי נתן seems to make it all about which came first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case of a stolen field, the buyer who improved it can usually collect his improvements only from the thief's unsold land. רבי נתן says this applies only when the thief sold other land before the improvements were made. If the improvements came first, the buyer can collect even from sold land, even though improvements are neither fixed nor written. This suggests the only reason is timing.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (brings a source)
When is this rule true?
His purchase
His improvements / added value
Property that was sold but still owed for an earlier debt
Apparently / this shows that

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two buyers straight: the 'first' bought the stolen field and improved it; the 'second' bought the thief's own land.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמַר רַבִּי נָתָן: אֵימָתַי –
phrases.english: Come and hear: Rabbi Natan said: When is this so –
phrases.notes: 'This' is the rule that a buyer of a stolen field cannot collect his improvements from sold property.

phrases.english: when the purchase of the second came first
before the improvements of the first;
but if the improvements of the first came first
before the purchase of the second –
he collects from liened property.
Apparently it is because it did not come first!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings another source on the original question of step 1. It suggests that neither a fixed amount nor writing is required, only that the obligation came first.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that collecting from sold property requires the obligation to be fixed and/or written.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי נתן lets the buyer collect from sold property if his improvements came first, so the rule seems to depend only on timing.

steps.title: It is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this is a dispute between תנאים, and quotes a ברייתא that says these debts are not collected from sold property because they are not written.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a dispute between תנאים, as it was taught: We do not collect from sold property for eaten produce, for improvements to land, or for the support of a wife and daughters, because of תיקון העולם, since these are not written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying רבי נתן is only one opinion. Another ברייתא gives a different reason: these debts are not written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן makes the rule about timing, but the ברייתא makes it about the debt not being written in any document. Since buyers cannot know about unwritten debts, taking land from them would hurt everyone, so the חכמים protected buyers. Because תנאים disagree, רבי נתן's view does not disprove the 'not written' reason.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute between תנאים
As it was taught in a ברייתא
Produce that was eaten (and must be paid back)
For the good order of the world
That they are not written in a document

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views: רבי נתן ties the rule to timing, while the ברייתא says these debts cannot be taken from buyers because they are not written.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why buyers are protected from hidden, unwritten debts: if they could lose land they bought to such debts, no one would buy land.

phrases.english: It is a dispute of tanna'im, as it is taught:
We do not take payment for eaten produce,
or for the improvement of land,
or for the support of a wife and daughters –
from liened property,
for the betterment of the world;
because they are not written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבי נתן in Step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי נתן proves the rule is only about timing.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי נתן is one view; another ברייתא holds the reason is that these debts are not written.

steps.title: רבי יוסי gives a different reason: the amounts are not fixed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. רבי יוסי rejects the reason "because they are not written" and says the real reason is that these debts have no fixed amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said: What fixing of the world is there in this? Isn't the real point that these debts are not of a fixed amount!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא it started in Step 18. Now we hear רבי יוסי's opinion, which shows that the תנאים argue about this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion said these debts are not collected from sold property because they are not written in a document. רבי יוסי says that is not the reason. A buyer could never know how big these debts might grow, so their open-ended amount is what protects the buyer. With two different reasons on record, the גמרא has shown that רבי נתן (Step 17) can follow one side of a real dispute between תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: Fixing of the world; a rule made for the good of society
Fixed, set in amount
But isn't it so that…

steps.whatToRemember: Two reasons are given for why some debts are not collected from sold property: "they are not written" (first opinion) or "their amount is not fixed" (רבי יוסי). This is a real dispute between תנאים.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said:

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מָה תִּיקּוּן הָעוֹלָם יֵשׁ בָּזוֹ?
phrases.english: And what fixing of the world is there in this?
phrases.notes: "This" means the first opinion's reason, that these debts are not collected because they are not written.

phrases.english: But aren't they not fixed in amount!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: וְכִי מָה תִּיקּוּן הָעוֹלָם יֵשׁ בָּזוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in Step 18 by giving the opposing opinion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The issue is a dispute between תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי נתן's view seemed to clash with the accepted reason about unwritten debts.
steps.terutzMaskana: תנאים argue about the reason (unwritten versus not fixed), so רבי נתן can follow one side.

steps.title: New topic: a finder of a lost object does not swear
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: one who finds a lost object does not take an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one who finds a lost object does not swear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה. This sets up רבי יצחק's teaching that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that someone who returns a lost object does not have to swear he kept nothing for himself. This is another rule made for תיקון העולם. The next step shows cases where the finder does have to swear.

keyTerms.meaning: A found object, a lost item that someone found
He will swear, take an oath

phrases.english: And one who finds a lost object does not swear.
phrases.notes: This quotes our משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה after the debt discussion ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who returns a lost object does not have to take an oath.

steps.title: רבי יצחק: tied pouches mean an oath, tied oxen do not
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that if the owner claims two tied pouches and the finder admits only one, the finder swears. With two tied oxen, the finder does not swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: If the owner says "You found two tied pouches of mine" and the finder says "I found only one," the finder swears. If the owner says "You found two tied oxen of mine" and the finder says "There was only one," the finder does not swear.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק gives two cases that look alike but have opposite rules. In both, the finder admits finding only part of what the owner claims.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, someone who admits part of a claim must swear about the rest. רבי יצחק says this applies to the tied pouches but not to the tied oxen. The גמרא will explain the difference in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: Pouches, money bags
Tied together
And the other one (here, the finder)
He swears, takes an oath

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix the two cases up. Pouches lead to an oath, oxen do not. Also, the finder in the pouch case swears even though the משנה said a finder does not swear.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
"You found two tied pouches of mine";
and the other one says:
"I found only one" — he swears.
"You found two tied oxen of mine";
and the other one says:
"There was only one" — he does not swear.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: שְׁנֵי כִּיסִין קְשׁוּרִין מָצָאתָ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives specific cases about a finder's oath, connected to the משנה's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A finder who admits one of two tied pouches swears. A finder who admits one of two tied oxen does not swear.

steps.title: Why are pouches different from oxen?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבי יצחק's distinction.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the pouch case and the oxen case have different rules. It is setting up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases look the same: two tied items are claimed and only one is admitted. So there must be some real difference between pouches and oxen.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רבי יצחק's two cases.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a finder swears about tied pouches but not about tied oxen.

steps.title: Oxen can come apart, pouches cannot
steps.stepSummary: Oxen can break loose from each other, so maybe only one was really there when he found it. Tied pouches do not come apart, so if he found one, he surely found both.
steps.simpleTranslation: Oxen come apart from each other. Pouches do not come apart from each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing to a simple fact about real life: tied oxen can pull apart, but tied pouches stay together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With oxen, the finder's story makes sense: the two oxen may have separated before he came, so his partial admission is believable and he does not swear. With pouches, it makes no sense that he found only one. That makes his denial suspicious, so he must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: They come apart, get separated
From each other

phrases.english: Oxen come apart from each other,
pouches do not come apart from each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Tied oxen can separate, so the finder's claim of finding one is believable. Tied pouches cannot separate, so finding one means finding both.

steps.title: A finder who says he returned one ox does swear
steps.stepSummary: If the finder admits he found both tied oxen but says he already gave one back, he swears.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the owner says "You found two tied oxen" and the finder says "I found them, and I gave one of them back to you," then he swears.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק adds another oxen case. Here the finder admits that he found both oxen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 21, the finder did not swear because the oxen might have separated before he came. Here he admits he found both, so that excuse no longer helps him. Now his only defense is his own claim that he returned one, and he must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: And I returned (it)
This person (introduces the ruling)

steps.whatToRemember: For tied oxen: if the finder says he found only one, he does not swear, since oxen come apart. If he admits finding both but says he returned one, he does swear.

phrases.english: "You found two tied oxen";
phrases.notes: This is still רבי יצחק speaking.

phrases.english: and the other one says:
"I found them, and I returned one of them to you"
— this one swears.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁנֵי שְׁווֹרִין קְשׁוּרִין מָצָאתָ וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר מָצָאתִי וְהֶחְזַרְתִּי לָךְ אֶחָד מֵהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a different oxen case where the finder does swear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A finder who admits finding both tied oxen but claims he returned one must swear.

steps.title: Challenge: Doesn't רבי יצחק accept that a finder does not swear?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יצחק can make a finder swear, when the משנה rules that a finder is free from an oath because of תיקון העולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק, doesn't he hold the rule "one who finds a lost object does not swear, because of תיקון העולם"?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יצחק's rulings. The משנה just said a finder does not swear, so how can רבי יצחק say he does?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our רבנן freed the finder from an oath so that people would not be scared off from returning lost things. רבי יצחק's cases, with two pouches or a returned ox, seem to bring back that very oath. So his rulings look like they go against an explicit משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not hold (this rule)
One who finds a lost object
He does not swear
Fixing the world: a rabbinic enactment for the good of society

steps.confusionAlert: This sounds like a question, but it is really a challenge. The גמרא is not asking for information. It is pointing out that רבי יצחק seems to go against the משנה.

phrases.english: And רבי יצחק, does he not hold
phrases.notes: This refers back to רבי יצחק's rulings in steps 21 and 24, where the finder has to swear.

phrases.english: "one who finds a lost object does not swear"
because of fixing the world"?!
phrases.notes: This is the line of our משנה quoted back in step 20.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יצחק's rulings in steps 21–24 by setting them against the משנה quoted in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יצחק's rulings that a finder must swear (two tied pouches, or claiming he returned one ox).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה frees a finder from an oath because of תיקון העולם. Requiring an oath in רבי יצחק's cases seems to contradict this enactment.
